prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B005 alone, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The chair asks what the lattice adds beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. My one-sentence answer is this. The comb made optical frequencies countable and the ion work showed how to control a single quantum absorber, but the magic-wavelength condition lets thousands of neutral atoms be held tightly enough (Lamb-Dicke regime) with the lattice light shift cancelled on the clock transition, so that motional and Stark systematics are removed without giving up the statistics of an ensemble. That is a conceptual step in how to isolate a quantum transition from its environment, not only a gain in averaging, and it is the reason the 1e-18 regime became reachable with stability that single ions cannot match. As a theorist working with superconducting circuits I know how much of the effort in any quantum device is about identifying and cancelling the dominant systematic, and the magic wavelength is a very clean example. The result is also mature in the sense I care about: independent reproduction at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, agreement between computed shifts and measurement, and comparisons over fibre links. On the question of waiting for the SI second, I agree with Olsson that the redefinition is a timetable set by metrology bodies, not a test of the physics. The physics is already demonstrated, so I would not delay. I considered whether to add a second part, but none of B015, B014 or B035 is both mature and bounded in credit as B005 is, and I will not add a part for the sake of balance.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real objection and I do not dismiss it. A skeptic can say the lattice clock is the best descendant of a recognised lineage and that a precision-measurement advance is a tool, not a discovery. My answer is that the discovery is how coherence can be preserved in a many-atom system at this level, but that answer depends on a narrow citation, and it fails if the text drifts toward metrology or the comb in general. The two-name attribution also leaves out contributors (Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Derevianko), and I cannot settle the priority chronology from the supplied material. Finally, the tightened bounds on constants and dark matter are limits, not detections, so the physical payoff is still partly prospective.

responses.point: Olsson says the committee should not wait for the SI second redefinition, since it is a policy timetable and not a test of the physics, and asks that Katori's 2001-2003 proposal be checked against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements.
responses.response: I accept your argument and I now drop the weight I put on the redefinition in round 1. The clock comparisons already show the performance, and an SI decision would add a calendar date, not scientific maturity. I agree with your request for a primary-source check, and I would make it a condition of the final vote: confirm Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first Sr lattice measurements, and Ye's accuracy results, from the papers. If that check shows a substantially earlier or parallel claim, I would want the committee to say so before voting, not after.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B005 from B043 and asks whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging, while keeping B014 and B015 as alternatives.
responses.response: The advance is conceptual, and I would put the argument in terms you will recognise as a theorist. A single ion is easy to isolate but has a poor signal-to-noise ratio per unit time. A neutral-atom ensemble would normally pay in light shifts and motional broadening, and the magic wavelength is what removes that cost. So averaging power and accuracy come together, not one at the expense of the other. On B015, I agree with your round-1 hesitation and I share it. The d-wave superconductivity payoff in the Hubbard model has not appeared, and the Zoller versus Esslinger seat is unresolved, so I keep B015 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll weighs the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as real but not decisive and says the lattice-clock concept is distinct from both, and he asks for credit to be narrower than the real history, which he notes includes ion-clock groups such as Schmidt and Rosenband.
responses.response: I agree with your weighting. I would add that the ion-clock groups you name are a reason to keep the ion and neutral-atom lineages separate in the citation, not a reason to add names. Al+ and other ion clocks reach their accuracy by a different route, and the lattice clock is credited for the magic-wavelength route. With a three-person cap and a clean two-name attribution, I prefer to say explicitly in the citation that it recognises the lattice clock, and to let the 2012 prize stand for ion control.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B005 first, observes that the 1e-18 clocks so far give only tightened bounds on constants and ultralight dark matter and not a detected variation, and keeps B035 and B014 as alternatives.
responses.response: You are right about the bounds and I have put it in my case against. I do not think a detection should be a precondition. The tests have already excluded parameter space that could not be reached before, and the gravitational redshift over millimetres is a direct measurement, not a bound. The next point is the citation. Your suggestion to avoid the comb lineage and my own point agree, so I propose the text above, which names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength step and does not mention metrology as a field.

uncertainties: Whether the primary-source check of Katori's 2001-2003 proposal against the first Sr lattice-clock measurements and Ye's accuracy results supports the two-name attribution without a priority conflict.
How much weight the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize should carry as overlap, which is a judgement of the committee and not something I can settle from the supplied material.
Whether a contributor such as Takamoto, Ludlow or Lemonde has a claim that a two-name prize would overlook.
I have not re-verified the latest accuracy figures against the primary papers and rely on my recollection and colleagues' statements.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers on superconducting circuits and microwave quantum optics, so I would flag a possible recusal issue for B046 (circuit QED) and for any superconducting-circuit quantum technology candidate. None of these is on the shortlist. I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or to the alternatives B015 and B014, so no specific conflict is apparent for the configuration I propose. Disclosure unchanged from round 1.
